explainedBy: Sequence (44-47): a junior copywriter in the agency brainstorm throws out clever lines; this beat opens the room with him pitching from his notes.

storyboard.claim: Picture a boardroom brainstorm at the same ad agency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield in the agency office, pitching from a page of notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the idea of 'the concept' into a concrete scene that will show it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the place (the agency) and the person who will pitch.

explainedBy: Same brainstorm: everyone is throwing out clever sentences; he jabs a line from his notes into the room, hunting a jingle for toothpaste.

storyboard.claim: Everyone throws out clever sentences, hunting a catchy jingle for a toothpaste or cleaner.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same copywriter, now pointing out a line from his notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; he goes from talking to throwing a line out (point).
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the product the room is pitching.

explainedBy: Same brainstorm: people shout slogans; he cheers his own line as if it were a winner.

storyboard.claim: Just spitballing: people shout slogans like 'gets dentures whiter'.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The copywriter celebrating his own slogan.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; pointing becomes celebrating his line.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the shouted slogans themselves are carried only by the audio.

explainedBy: Same room, the change: the veteran pro, unmoved, points at the junior's clever line — without a concept it is worthless — and the junior is caught off guard.

storyboard.claim: The veteran pros know that without a concept a clever sentence is worthless.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The grey-haired veteran ad man, unimpressed, pointing at the surprised junior.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the veteran enters and the junior's cheer turns to surprise.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the verdict coming from the experienced side of the room.

explainedBy: Order of operations: the big idea comes first, the clever copy after it.

storyboard.claim: A concept isn't a slogan: the big idea always comes before the clever copy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: The big idea -> Clever copy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The veteran's verdict stated as a rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the sequence (idea first, words second) visible.

explainedBy: Why writing fails: the writer holds out pages of mere words and the audience, unmoved, walks away.

storyboard.claim: Failed novels and pitches fail because they have no concept, just words.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The writer reaching out his pages; the reader in red walks off with a blank face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the rule to its consequence: words without a concept lose the audience.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the failure as the audience leaving.

explainedBy: Sequence (50-51): a concept is a lens on the product; the veteran picks up the magnifying glass as he names the frame of reference.

storyboard.claim: A concept establishes a frame of reference greater than the product itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran ad man picks up a magnifying glass.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From what fails to what a concept does.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lens object introduces the 'look at it differently' idea.

explainedBy: Same lens: looking through it, the material is seen with fresh eyes — not handed over as raw data.

storyboard.claim: The concept's spin forces the audience to see the material with fresh eyes; raw data is not enough.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran holding the magnifier, face lit up in surprise.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; he now holds the lens and his face shows the new view.
storyboard.addedInformation: The surprised face shows what 'fresh eyes' feels like.

explainedBy: Not features or a chronology handed over raw: the raw data has to pass through the lens.

storyboard.claim: Don't list features or events in order — provide the lens.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Raw data -> The lens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the lens idea as a step the writer must add.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the raw list with the framed version.

explainedBy: Pressfield introduces his proof — a devious advertising example — with the diamond ring that it is about.

storyboard.claim: Pressfield proves this with one of the most devious examples in advertising history.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield, smirking, beside a diamond engagement ring.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the principle to the example.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ring previews the example before it is named.

callout.text: A shiny rock like any other

explainedBy: The starting point of the De Beers story: the diamond ring as a plain shiny commodity.

storyboard.claim: For a long time diamonds were just another shiny commodity — why a diamond for an engagement ring?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The diamond ring alone.
storyboard.onScreenText: A shiny rock like any other
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The example named: De Beers diamonds.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the product before any concept.

explainedBy: Comparison: diamond, ruby and sapphire side by side, all just shiny rocks.

storyboard.claim: Why not a ruby or a sapphire? They are all shiny rocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter with three equal buckets: Diamond, Ruby, Sapphire.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The diamond placed among its rivals.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows there is no built-in reason to prefer the diamond.

explainedBy: Sequence (56-57): the ad makers' concept lands — the veteran celebrates over the ring as 'A diamond is forever' appears.

storyboard.claim: Instead of copy about shine, De Beers introduced a concept: A diamond is forever.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The ad man celebrating beside the diamond ring.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From 'all shiny rocks' to the concept that singles out one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the famous line on the ring.

explainedBy: Same ring: he points at the stone itself — its physical indestructibility, the hardest material.

storyboard.claim: They took the stone's physical indestructibility — the hardest material — and enlisted it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The ad man pointing at the diamond ring.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; celebrating becomes pointing at the stone's property.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the physical fact the concept is built on.

explainedBy: The mechanism of the concept: the physical property becomes the symbol — indestructible stone -> everlasting love.

storyboard.claim: The physical property becomes a symbol for everlasting love — that is a concept.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Indestructible stone -> Everlasting love.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the move begun on the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the transfer of meaning that makes the concept.

explainedBy: Sequence (59-60): a young man offers his fiancee a gift ring that is not a diamond; this beat is the offer.

storyboard.claim: The frame is so strong that buying your fiancee any other kind of ring sends a message.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A young man happily holding out a gift box to a woman.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the mechanism to what it does to a buyer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the purchase the concept judges.

explainedBy: Same couple, the result: the ruby or pearl reads as 'temporary love' — she slumps, hurt, and his smile turns to worry.

storyboard.claim: A ruby or a pearl essentially says your love is temporary.
storyboard.concreteVisual: She slumps, sad; he holds the gift, worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the offer turns into her hurt and his worry.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the concept's power as a reaction between two people.

explainedBy: What the concept anchors to: not logic but love — a primal human desire.

storyboard.claim: They bypass the logical brain and anchor the product to a primal human desire.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A heart icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the couple's hurt to the desire the ad hooks into.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names love as the anchor.

explainedBy: The diamond ring alone on screen: its concept leaves competing stones no answer.

storyboard.claim: The concept renders competing points of view moot — not a fair fight. Avis did the same.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The diamond ring alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Verdict on the De Beers example.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the Avis turn at the end of the beat is left to the next beats.

explainedBy: The glaring negative: Avis sorted second behind Hertz.

storyboard.claim: Avis's 'We're number two' took a glaring negative: losing to Hertz.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: Hertz: number one | Avis: number two.
storyboard.onScreenText: Hertz: number one | Avis: number two
storyboard.relationToPrevious: A second advertising example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the ranking Avis had to work with.

explainedBy: The spin: second best turned into a promise of superior customer service.

storyboard.claim: They spun the negative into a positive concept about superior customer service.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Second best -> Superior service.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the ranking to the concept built on it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the negative becoming the selling point.

explainedBy: From ads to Hollywood: the clapperboard marks the era of the high-concept movie.

storyboard.claim: The 80s and 90s were the era of the high-concept movie, like Die Hard.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A film clapperboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The concept idea moves from advertising to movies.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the new field: film.

explainedBy: Sequence (66-67): the Die Hard concept as a picture — a cop, afraid, trapped among the high-rise towers.

storyboard.claim: Die Hard: a blue-collar cop trapped in a high-rise with armed terrorists — there's your movie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A uniformed cop, afraid, in front of high-rise towers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The high-concept example made concrete.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cop and the building the concept names.

explainedBy: Same cop and towers: from the concept alone you can feel the movie — his fear turns into the hunched claustrophobia.

storyboard.claim: You see the elevator-shaft fights, hear the wisecracks, feel the claustrophobia.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The cop hunched and worried before the towers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; fear becomes a hunched, cornered body.
storyboard.addedInformation: The body shows the feeling the concept delivers.

explainedBy: A Hollywood term is introduced: the clapperboard with the jargon 'pull outs'.

storyboard.claim: Once a concept is proven, you get what Hollywood calls pull outs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The clapperboard again.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From one concept to its copies.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the industry term.

explainedBy: The definition as a mechanism: a proven concept applied to a new scenario to milk the same response.

storyboard.claim: A pull out takes a proven concept and applies it to a slightly different scenario for the same response.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow: Proven concept -> New scenario -> Same response.
storyboard.onScreenText: Proven concept -> New scenario -> Same response
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the term just introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the three steps of a pull out.

explainedBy: Sequence (70-71): the pull outs listed as copies of one concept — first Die Hard and Die Hard on a plane.

storyboard.claim: If the concept is Die Hard, the pull out is Passenger 57: Die Hard on a plane.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: Die Hard | On a plane.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The definition applied to Die Hard.
storyboard.addedInformation: First example of a pull out.

explainedBy: Same sorter, two more copies: on a battleship (Under Siege) and in a flooded town (Hard Rain).

storyboard.claim: Under Siege is Die Hard on a battleship; Hard Rain, in a flooded town. The concept is a master key.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sorter grows: On a battleship, In a flooded town.
storyboard.onScreenText: On a battleship | In a flooded town
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same diagram; two more buckets added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows one concept reused again and again.

explainedBy: The concept as the master key just named: one key reused on a new door, no new invention needed.

storyboard.claim: You don't reinvent the wheel; you apply the concept to a new setting. But how does this apply to ordinary writers?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A key.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the 'master key' image from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the host's turn to ordinary listeners is left to the next beat.

callout.text: A history paper on the Civil War

explainedBy: Sequence (73-76): an ordinary writer at his desk with a factual paper; does it really need a concept? Pressfield says yes.

storyboard.claim: Say I'm an analyst writing a Q3 memo or a sophomore writing a Civil War history paper.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An ordinary writer at his desk holding his paper.
storyboard.onScreenText: A history paper on the Civil War
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Hollywood to everyday writing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts an everyday writer and his paper on screen.

explainedBy: Same writer: the doubt — does a plain factual paper really need a concept? He sags over his pages.

storyboard.claim: Does a spreadsheet or a basic historical essay really need a concept?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The writer slumps, worried, over his paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the neutral writer becomes doubtful.
storyboard.addedInformation: The slump shows the 'heavy lifting' doubt.

callout.text: Pressfield does not budge on this

explainedBy: Same desk, the answer arrives: Pressfield points at the doubting writer — no exceptions — and the writer is taken aback.

storyboard.claim: It feels like heavy lifting for factual writing, but Pressfield is uncompromising.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield points at the surprised writer.
storyboard.onScreenText: Pressfield does not budge on this
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; Pressfield enters and answers the doubt.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who settles the question and how firmly.

explainedBy: Same pair: Pressfield explains the rule — every piece of communication needs a concept — and the writer listens.

storyboard.claim: Every single piece of communication needs a concept — even a diet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield talking to the listening writer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the pointing becomes explaining, the writer calms.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the rule's scope.

explainedBy: Sequence (77-78): everyday things that each have a concept — a diet, an invasion.

storyboard.claim: Atkins: carbs are the enemy. An invasion: weapons of mass destruction, or liberation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter: Atkins diet | Invasion.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Examples of the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the concept outside writing.

explainedBy: Same sorter, one more: even a salad restaurant has a concept.

storyboard.claim: A salad restaurant has a concept — and a Civil War paper cannot just be...
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sorter adds Salad restaurant.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same diagram; one more bucket.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes the everyday list.

explainedBy: Sequence (79-81): the professor grading a paper — first a bare timeline of 1863 that she reads with a blank face, because nobody wants to read raw data.

storyboard.claim: A timeline of 1863 is raw data nobody wants to read; a concept like railroad gauges deciding the war is not.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The professor holds a paper with a bored, blank face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the rule to the Civil War paper.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the reader's reaction to raw data.

callout.text: Refining the raw ore into gold

explainedBy: Same professor, the change: with the concept the facts become gold — her blank face turns to surprise.

storyboard.claim: With the concept you aren't reciting facts; you refine the raw ore into gold.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The professor, now surprised, reading the paper.
storyboard.onScreenText: Refining the raw ore into gold
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; bored becomes surprised.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the effect of the concept on the reader.

explainedBy: Same professor, the result: she picks up the lens the concept gave her and reads with pleasure — the writer respected her time.

storyboard.claim: You've given the professor a fascinating lens on what she already knows — respecting the reader's time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The professor, happy, picks up a magnifying glass.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; she swaps the paper for the lens and smiles.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties back to the lens idea from beat 50.
